L542: #### Green’s relations
L543: 
L544: It is easy to verify that $f_{Y,Z}f_{X,Y}=f_{X,Z}$ so $f_{X,Y}f_{Y,X}f_{X,Y}=f_{X,Y}$ and therefore $\OF_{n}$ is a regular monoid. As a regular submonoid of $\T_{n}$ it is easy to describe its $\Rc$ and $\Lc$ relations, as explained in the previous example (see [cite43†12 , Proposition 2.4.2]). The $\Rc$ and $\Lc$ relations of $\T_{n}$ can be found in [cite43†12 , Excercise 16 on page 63].
L545: ###### Lemma 4.5.
L546: 
L547: Let $f_{X,Y},f_{Z,W}\in\OF_{n}$, then
L548: 
L549:  | $\displaystyle f_{X,Y}\,\Rc\,f_{Z,W}$  | $\displaystyle\iff\im(f_{X,Y})=\im(f_{Z,W})\iff Y=W$  |
L550:  | $\displaystyle f_{X,Y}\,\Lc\,f_{Z,W}$  | $\displaystyle\iff\ker(f_{X,Y})=\ker(f_{Z,W})\iff X=Z.$  |
L551: 
L552: It follows immediately that $f_{X,Y}\,\Hc\,f_{Z,W}\iff f_{X,Y}=f_{Z,W}$ so $\OF_{n}$ is an $\Hc$-trivial monoid (which is also clear from the fact that $\OF_{n}$ is a regular submonoid of $\Op_{n}$). In particular, it has only trivial subgroups.
L553: Next, we turn to describe the $\Jc$-classes. Recall that the rank of a function $f$ is the size of its image. For $f_{X,Y}\in\OF_{n}$ we have $\rank(f_{X,Y})=|X|+1=|Y|+1$.
L554: ###### Lemma 4.6.
L555: 
L556: Let $f_{X,Y},f_{Z,W}\in\OF_{n}$ then $f_{X,Y}\,\Jc\,f_{Z,W}\iff\rank(f_{X,Y})=\rank(f_{Z,W})$.
L557: ###### Proof.
L558: 
L559: Since $\OF_{n}$ is a finite monoid we know that $\Jc=\Rc\circ\Lc=\Lc\circ\Rc$ (see [cite43†12 , Proposition 2.1.4]). Now cite66†4.5 implies that
L560: 
L561:  | $$f_{X,Y}\,\Jc\,f_{Z,W}\iff f_{X,Y}\,\Rc\,f_{Z,Y}\,\Lc\,f_{Z,W}\iff|Z|=|Y|\iff\rank(f_{X,Y})=\rank(f_{Z,W}).$$  |
L562: 
L563: ∎
L564: In conclusion, we obtain a neat description for the “eggbox” diagrams of $\OF_{n}$ (see [cite43†12 , Section 2.2] for the meaning of an “eggbox” diagram). The monoid $\OF_{n}$ has $n$ $\Jc$-classes. For every $0\leq k\leq n-1$ we can associate a $\Jc$-class $J_{k}$ of all functions $f_{X,Y}$ such that $|X|=|Y|=k$. Both the $\Rc$-classes and the $\Lc$-classes in $J_{k}$ are indexed by subsets $Z\subseteq[n-1]$ with $|Z|=k$. For every $Z\subseteq[n-1]$ with $|Z|=k$ we have an $\Rc$-class
L565:  | $$R_{Z}=\{f_{X,Z}\mid X\subseteq[n-1],\quad|X|=|Z|\}$$  |
L566: 
L567: and an $\Lc$-class
L568: 
L569:  | $$L_{Z}=\{f_{Z,Y}\mid Y\subseteq[n-1],\quad|Y|=|Z|\}.$$  |
L570: 
L571: Every $\Hc$-class contains one element. Every $\Lc$-class ($\Rc$-class) in $J_{k}$ contains ${n-1\choose k}$ elements. The $\Jc$-class $J_{k}$ contains ${n-1\choose k}$ $\Lc$-classes ($\Rc$-classes) and a total of ${n-1\choose k}^{2}$ elements.
L572: #### Reduced $E$-Fountain structure
L573: 
L574: Set $E=\{f_{X,X}\mid X\subseteq[n-1]\}\subseteq E(\OF_{n})$. Note that $E$ does not contain all the idempotents of $\OF_{n}$, but it is precisely the set of idempotents of $\C_{n}$. According to cite66†4.5 , we know that
L575: 
L576:  | $$f_{Y,Y}\,\Rc\,f_{X,Y}\,\Lc\,f_{X,X}$$  |
L577: for every $X,Y\subseteq[n-1]$ with $|X|=|Y|$. Therefore, every $\Lc$-class and every $\Rc$-class contains an element of $E$. Since $\Lc\subseteq\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{E}$ and $\Rc\subseteq\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}_{E}$, we deduce that every $\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{E}$-class and every $\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}_{E}$-class contains an element of $E$ so $\OF_{n}$ is an $E$-Fountain semigroup.
L578: Now, it is well-known (see [cite67†3 , Lemma 3.6]) that the idempotents of a $\Jc$-trivial semigroup satisfy the property that $ef=e$ if and only if $fe=e$. Since $E$ is the set of idempotents of the $\Jc$-trivial semigroup $\C_{n}$ we obtain that $\OF_{n}$ is in fact a reduced $E$-Fountain semigroup. Note that
L579:  | $$(f_{X,Y})^{\ast}=f_{X,X},\quad(f_{X,Y})^{+}=f_{Y,Y}$$  |
L580: 
L581: and therefore
L582: 
L583:  | $$f_{X,Y}\,\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{E}\,f_{Z,W}\iff X=Z,\quad f_{X,Y}\,\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}_{E}\,f_{Z,W}\iff Y=W.$$  |
L584: 
L585: In particular we have
L586: 
L587:  | $$\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{E}=\Lc,\quad\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}_{E}=\Rc.$$  |
L588: As in the previous example, this immediately implies that $\OF_{n}$ satisfies the congruence condition (by [cite43†12 , Proposition 2.1.2]) and both the right and left generalized ample conditions (by cite61†3.5 ). The congruence condition implies that $\OF_{n}$ has an associated category $\mathcal{C}(\OF_{n})$.
L589: The objects of $\mathcal{C}(\OF_{n})$ are in one-to one correspondence with sets $X\subseteq[n-1].$ Every $f_{X,Y}\in\OF_{n}$ corresponds to a morphism from $X$ to $Y$ so there exists a (unique) morphism from $X$ to $Y$ if and only if $|X|=|Y|$. In other words, $\mathcal{C}(\OF_{n})$ represent the equivalence relation $\sim$ defined on subsets of $[n-1]$ by $X\sim Y\iff|X|=|Y|$.
L590: Two objects $X,Y\subseteq[n-1]$ are isomorphic if and only if $|X|=|Y|$ and in this case there is a unique morphism from $X$ to $Y$. In particular, $\mathcal{C}(\OF_{n})$ is both a groupoid and a locally trivial category - where a locally trivial category is a category whose only endomorphisms (i.e., morphisms whose domain and range are equal) are the identity morphisms.
L591: Since the Catalan monoid $\C_{n}$ is a submonoid of $\OF_{n}$ and $E\subseteq\C_{n}$ it is also clear that $\C_{n}$ satisfies the right and left generalized ample identities. This is a much neater proof of this fact than the one given in [cite23†28 ].
L592: #### The semigroup algebra
L593: 
L594: Define a partial order $\preceq$ on $\OF_{n}$ by
L595: 
L596:  | $$\mbox{$f_{Z,W}\preceq f_{X,Y}\iff W\subsetneqq Y$}\text{ or }\mbox{$(W=Y\text{ and }Z\leq X)$}.$$  |
L597: 
L598: Note that this is equivalent to
L599: 
L600:  | $f_{Z,W}\preceq f_{X,Y}\iff\im(f_{Z,W})\subsetneqq\im(f_{X,Y})$ or $(\im(f_{Z,W})=\im(f_{X,Y})\text{ and }Z\leq X)$  |
L601: It is easy to verify that this is indeed a partial order (it is the lexicographic order on the Cartesian product of $\subseteq$ and $\leq$). Recall that the relation $\trianglelefteq_{l}$ is defined on a reduced $E$-Fountain semigroup by the rule that $a\trianglelefteq_{l}b$ if and only if $a=be$ for some $e\in E$.
L602: ###### Lemma 4.7.
L603: 
L604: In the semigroup $\OF_{n}$, there is a containment of relations $\trianglelefteq_{l}\subseteq\preceq$.
L605: ###### Proof.
L606: 
L607: Let $f_{X,Y}\in\OF_{n}$ and $f_{Z,Z}\in E$. We need to show that $f_{X,Y}f_{Z,Z}\preceq f_{X,Y}.$ First, note that $\im(f_{X,Y}f_{Z,Z})\subseteq\im(f_{X,Y})=Y\cup\{n\}$. If $\im(f_{X,Y}f_{Z,Z})\subsetneqq Y\cup\{n\}$ then we are done. It is left to consider the option that $\im(f_{X,Y}f_{Z,Z})=Y\cup\{n\}$. In other words we assume that $f_{X,Y}f_{Z,Z}\,\Rc\,f_{X,Y}$. The fact that $\Rc$ is a left congruence implies that
L608:  | $$f_{X,X}f_{Z,Z}=f_{Y,X}f_{X,Y}f_{Z,Z}\,\Rc\,f_{Y,X}f_{X,Y}=f_{X,X}$$  |
L609: 
L610: so
L611: 
L612:  | $$\im(f_{X,X}f_{Z,Z})=X\cup\{n\}.$$  |
L613: 
L614: Therefore, we can write
L615: 
L616:  | $$f_{X,X}f_{Z,Z}=f_{Z^{\prime},X}$$  |
L617: 
L618: and observe that $f_{X,X},f_{Z,Z}\in\C_{n}$ so $f_{Z^{\prime},X}\in\C_{n}$ as well hence $Z^{\prime}\leq X$. Finally,
L619: 
L620:  | $$f_{X,Y}f_{Z,Z}=f_{X,Y}f_{X,X}f_{Z,Z}=f_{X,Y}f_{Z^{\prime},X}=f_{Z^{\prime},Y}.$$  |
L621: 
L622: and therefore $f_{X,Y}f_{Z,Z}\preceq f_{X,Y}$ as required. ∎
L623: cite49†3.2 and cite68†4.7 implies that for every field $\Bbbk$ we have an isomorphism of algebras
L624: 
L625:  | $$\Bbbk\OF_{n}\simeq\Bbbk\mathcal{C}(\OF_{n}).$$  |
L626: 
L627: This isomorphism allows us to obtain a lot of information on the algebra $\Bbbk\OF_{n}$. For instance we have the following immediate corollary:
L628: ###### Lemma 4.8.
L629: 
L630: For every field $\Bbbk$ the algebra $\Bbbk\OF_{n}$ is semisimple.
L631: ###### Proof.
L632: 
L633: It is well-known that the algebra $\Bbbk\mathcal{G}$ of a finite groupoid $\mathcal{G}$ is semisimple if and only if the order of every endomorphism group is invertible in $\Bbbk$ ([cite34†31 , Theorem 8.15]). In our case, the endomorphism groups of $\mathcal{C}(\OF_{n})$ are trivial so $\Bbbk\mathcal{C}(\OF_{n})$ is semisimple for every field $\Bbbk$ and hence also so is $\Bbbk\OF_{n}$. ∎
L634: We remark that not many examples are known for non-inverse semigroups with a semisimple algebra. Another notable example is the semigroup of matrices over a finite field of appropriate characteristic (see [cite34†31 , Section 5.6]).
L635: #### The monoid of order-preserving partial permutations
L636: Recall that the symmetric inverse monoid $\IS_{n}$ is the monoid of all partial permutations on the set $[n]$. Our next observation is related to the submonoid $\IO_{n}$ of all order-preserving partial permutations (also denoted sometimes $\POI_{n}$- see [cite69†4 , cite70†5 , cite71†7 ]). In other words, $\IO_{n}$ consists of all partial permutations $\theta:[n]\to[n]$ such that $\theta(i)<\theta(j)$ if $i,j$ are in the domain of $\theta$ and $i<j$.
L637: It is clear that every $\theta\in\IO_{n}$ is completely determined by its domain and image. In the other direction, given $X,Y\subseteq[n]$ such that $|X|=|Y|$ there exists a unique $\theta_{X,Y}\in\IO_{n}$ whose domain is $X$ and image is $Y$. Therefore, elements of $\IO_{n}$ can also be indexed by pairs of sets $X,Y\subseteq[n]$ such that $|X|=|Y|$.
L638: It is well-known that $\IO_{n}$ is an inverse semigroup so in particular, it is a reduced $E$-Fountain semigroup for $E=E(\IO_{n})$ which satisfies the congruence condition. Moreover, its idempotents commute and it satisfies the left and right ample conditions. Consider the associated category $\mathcal{C}(\IO_{n})$ (which is in fact an inductive groupoid - see [cite72†17 , Chapter 4]). It is easy to deduce that the categories $\mathcal{C}(\IO_{n})$ and $\mathcal{C}(\OF_{n+1})$ are isomorphic.
L639: Indeed, the idempotents of $\IO_{n}$ are the partial permutations of the form $\theta_{X,X}$ - where the domain equals the image. In other words these are precisely the partial identities. So objects of $\mathcal{C}(\IO_{n})$ are in one to one correspondence with sets $X\subseteq[n]$. For every $\theta\in\IO_{n}$ there exists a unique morphism $C(\theta)$ from the domain of $\theta$ to its image. So the isomorphism between $\mathcal{C}(\IO_{n})$ and $\mathcal{C}(\OF_{n+1})$ is clear.
L640: According to cite49†3.2 (which for the case of inverse semigroups is precisely [cite32†29 , Theorem 4.2]) we know that $\Bbbk\mathcal{C}(\IO_{n})\simeq\Bbbk\IO_{n}$ for every field $\Bbbk$. So we end up with the following result.
L641: ###### Proposition 4.9.
L642: 
L643: Let $\Bbbk$ be a field, there is an isomorphism of algebras
L644: 
L645:  | $$\Bbbk\OF_{n+1}\simeq\Bbbk\IO_{n}.$$  |
L646: ###### Remark 4.10.
L647: 
L648: Note that we have an explicit description of this isomorphism. An isomorphism $\varphi:\Bbbk\OF_{n+1}\to\Bbbk\mathcal{C}(\OF_{n+1})$ is given in cite49†3.2 and according to [cite32†29 ], an isomorphism $\psi:\mathcal{C}(\Bbbk\IO_{n})\to\Bbbk\IO_{n}$ can be defined by
L649: 
L650:  | $$\psi(C(\theta))=\sum_{\tau\leq\theta}\mu(\tau,\theta)\tau$$  |
L651: 
L652: where $\leq$ is the standard partial order on an inverse semigroup and $\mu$ is its related Möbius function (see [cite63†22 , Chapter 3]).
L653: As a final observation, we note that a similar isomorphism holds for certain submonoids. Consider the Catalan monoid $\C_{n}\subseteq\OF_{n}$. The objects of $\mathcal{C}(\C_{n})$ are sets $X\subseteq[n-1]$ and there is a unique morphism from $X$ to $Y$ if ($|X|=|Y|$ and) $X\leq Y$. Now consider the monoid $\IC_{n}\subseteq\IO_{n}$ of all order-preserving and order-increasing partial permutations (see [cite64†8 , Chapter 14]).
L654: In other words, a partial permutation $\theta$ belongs to $\IC_{n}$ if $\theta\in\IO_{n}$ and $i\leq\theta(i)$ for every $i$ in the domain of $\theta$. The semigroup $\IC_{n}$ is not inverse. However, since $E(\IC_{n})=E(\IO_{n})$ it is clear that it is a reduced $E$-Fountain semigroup which satisfies both the congruence and the right\left ample conditions. It is also clear that $\theta_{X,Y}\in\IO_{n}$ belongs to $\IC_{n}$ if and only if $X\leq Y$.
L655: Therefore, $\mathcal{C}(\IC_{n})$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal{C}(\C_{n+1})$ and we obtain:
L656: ###### Corollary 4.11.
L657: 
L658: ^{3}^{3} 3 This is an unpublished observation of the authors of [cite28†19 ] (private communication).
L659: 
L660: Let $\Bbbk$ be a field, there is an isomorphism of algebras
L661: 
L662:  | $$\Bbbk\C_{n+1}\simeq\Bbbk\IC_{n}.$$  |

L9: # Title:Algebras of reduced $E$-Fountain semigroups and the generalized ample identity II

L15: cite7†View PDF cite8†HTML (experimental) L16: > Abstract:We study the generalized right ample identity, introduced by the author in a previous paper. Let $S$ be a reduced $E$-Fountain semigroup which satisfies the congruence condition. We can associate with $S$ a small category $\mathcal{C}(S)$ whose set of objects is identified with the set $E$ of idempotents and its morphisms correspond to elements of $S$.
L17: We prove that $S$ satisfies the generalized right ample identity if and only if every element of $S$ induces a homomorphism of left $S$-actions between certain classes of generalized Green's relations. In this case, we interpret the associated category $\mathcal{C}(S)$ as a discrete form of a Peirce decomposition of the semigroup algebra. We also give some natural examples of semigroups satisfying this identity.
